g.text: DHT11 - the protocol engine on both sides
start signal + acknowledge + 40 timed bits; the bit value IS the width
SENSOR SIDE - tb/tb_pe_soc_dht11.v
ARM
the model waits for the start signal:
low > 18 ms, then the host's 20-40 us high
by WATCHING pin_oe, not the line.
the release is unmeasurable on the line
ACK
80 low, 80 high
the sensor pulls the line low for 80 us
and high for 80 us. The firmware never times
this - it is skipped by the edge-wait loop.
BITS
40 of them
per bit: 50 us low, then the release.
0 = 28 us of high (the SHORT end of its own
26-28 us window - a sensor inside its
specification)
1 = 70 us of high
then the bus hold, 50 us, after bit 39.
SAMPLE
the margin check
for every one of the 40 bits: the host's
sample must land AFTER the longest 0-release
ends and BEFORE the 1-release ends.
measured margin: 17.0 us and 25.0 us
CHECK
what is claimed
1. the start signal is > 18 000 us
2. the host window is inside 20..40 us
3. the host RELEASED - measured on pin_oe,
because the pull-up holds the line high
throughout and the release moves nothing
6. the checksum: (2c+01+aa+55) & 0xff == 2c
7. every sample is inside its window
8. >= 20 of the 39 bit-transitions are real
FIRMWARE SIDE - firmware/dht11_read.pe
CLAIM
PINOE = 0x00 (release), TXPIN = DHT_DATA,
PINOE = DHT_DATA (claim one pad, push-pull)
the idle state is the pull-up
START
the line goes low
dmem[11] = 0 (the byte index), dmem[15] = 0
TXPIN = 0x00, dmem[7] = 0 (the delay's
return phase)
LONG pair (6,255), n1 = 212: one outer step
is 5145 clocks = 85.8 us
18 ms = 1.08 M clocks, the longest single
timed interval in the project
PH0
the host's high window
TXPIN = DHT_DATA - pull HIGH, do not
merely release, and this step is not optional:
the sensor pulls the line LOW to answer, so
the host cannot just stop driving and let the
pull-up win. dmem[7] = 1
FINE pair (2,6), n1 = 45: 30 us
the 20-40 us window, aimed at 30
PH1
RELEASE
PINOE = 0x00 - the pull-up owns the line.
dmem[7] = 2
FINE pair, n1 = 250: a COARSE 170 us, not a
deadline. It only has to be late enough not
to be fooled by the acknowledge's 80 us of
high, and early enough to still be inside bit
0's low prefix.
The edge waits below correct the rest
PH2
the acknowledge is in flight
dmem[7] = 3, then JMP ph3
the acknowledge is not timed, it is SKIPPED
by falling into the same edge-wait loop: the
first round waits out the 80/80 us ack and
the second one is bit 0
PH3
synchronise, then aim
w_lo: spin until the line is LOW
the next bit's 50 us prefix.
A 0 sampled late is already low and
passes through at once.
w_hi: spin until the line is HIGH
the RELEASE - which is the bit's value
window: 26-28 us for a 0, 70 us for a 1.
THE HOST CANNOT SAMPLE INSIDE THE
RELEASE: 20 us in is both a 0 and a 1.
then 45 us (FINE, n1 = 67), dmem[7] = 4
PH4
SAMPLE ONCE
IN A, PIN; AND A, DHT_DATA
the sample arrives in BIT 6 and a DHT11 byte
is MSB first, so it must reach bit 7. There
is no shift-left in this ISA:
MOV X,A / ADD A,X = 0x00->0x00, 0x40->0x80
exact for one bit because 0x40+0x40 = 0x80
does not carry out of the byte.
then: acc = 2*acc (+1 if the sample was 1)
dmem[5]-- ; eight times and the byte is banked
at dmem[0..4] by STS [X], A
X IS USED AS SCRATCH HERE, WHICH THE ISA'S OWN
HEADER SAYS NOT TO DO - so the byte index
lives in dmem[11] and is reloaded before every
STS. Keeping it in X silently banks every byte
at the accumulator's own value: the frame comes
out 00 02 00 00 08, which looks like a dead sensor.
DLY1/DLY2/DLY3
the delay
BOTH inner counters are RELOADED from their
targets (dmem[12], dmem[14]) every pass. The
routine cannot RETURN to five addresses and
the ISA has no indirect jump, so dmem[7] is the
phase and a subtract chain dispatches it.
TWO (n2,n3) pairs, because the ratio between the
shortest and longest delay here is 34 000 to 1:
long (6,255) one step 5145 clocks = 85.8 us
short (2,6) one step 41 clocks = 0.68 us
A single pair cannot do both: with the fine step
the 18 ms start needs an outer counter of 11 900,
and with the coarse step the 30 us window could not
be AIMED at - 20.7 us would be inside the 20-40 us
window and 34 us would be outside it.
PARK
done
dmem[15] = 1 - all 40 bits are in. THE
PROGRAM'S OBSERVABLE OUTPUT, so a testbench
can tell "hung mid-byte" (0) from "finished".
TXPIN = 0x00, then JMP halt: the ISA has no HALT.
dmem[7] == 0
dmem[7] == 1
dmem[7] == 2
the release has been seen
dmem[7] == 4
dmem[5] != 0
the byte is banked, dmem[8]--, and if any are left there are eight more bits
dmem[8] == 0
Why the host synchronises instead of counting.
A 0-bit is 50 + 26..28 = 76..78 us and a 1-bit
is 50 + 70 = 120 us. A host that waited a fixed
time per bit, computed from the previous bit's
value, would track the sensor exactly for a
while and then drift: at the 2 us spread of the
0-bit, twenty zero bits is 40 us of slip, which
is three times the margin.
That WAS this program's first design, and it
decoded the nominal frame perfectly while
failing as soon as the sensor was modelled at
the SHORT end of its own 0-bit window - a
sensor inside its specification and the
firmware outside its own.
That is the whole difference between a
bit-banger that works on the bench and one that
works on a shelf.
Why 45 us and not 20 us.
The host cannot sample inside the release: a
line high 20 us into the release is a 0 AND a 1.
The two differ only AFTERWARDS - a 0's release
ends at 28 us and the next bit pulls the line
low again, while a 1's runs to 70 us. So the
sample has to be in that gap, and 45 us is
aimed there: 17 us of margin on the 0 side and
25 us on the 1 side.
This is the ONE place in the program where a
timing number has to be AIMED rather than
merely satisfied. The 18 ms start and the 30 us
host window only have to be inside their windows.
the start signal is seen
the host starts again
(the program reads once and parks)
